reason: The narrative presents non-leaders as having significant agency. Most strikingly, Jael (described simply as 'the wife of Heber the Kenite,' not a leader) independently makes the decision to invite Sisera into her tent, provide him hospitality, and then deliberately kill him by driving a tent peg through his head while he sleeps. The text explicitly emphasizes this: 'by the hand of a woman shall the Lord sell Sisera' (כִּ֣י בְֽיַד־ אִשָּׁ֔ה יִמְכֹּ֥ר יְהוָ֖ה אֶת־ סִֽיסְרָ֑א). Additionally, the children of Israel (as a collective non-leadership body) exercise agency by crying out to God. These actions demonstrate that non-leaders have decisive agency in shaping the narrative outcome.
